title: Romeo and Juliet
author: William Shakespeare
openingText: Two households, both alike in dignity, in fair Verona, where we lay our scene, from ancient grudge break to new mutiny, where civil blood makes civil hands unclean. From forth the fatal loins of these two foes a pair of star-cross'd lovers take their life; whose misadventured piteous overthrows do with their death bury their parents' strife.
about: Two teenagers from warring families meet at a party on Sunday and are dead by Friday. Shakespeare tells you this in the prologue. The tragedy isn't the surprise — it's the speed, and watching every character make the choice that makes it inevitable.

angleCards.title: Who is actually responsible?
angleCards.text: The prologue blames the stars. The families blame each other. But Romeo and Juliet make choices — fast, reckless, irreversible ones. I want to watch where the real cause of the tragedy lies, and whether Shakespeare lets anyone off the hook.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand whether the tragedy is caused by fate, by the feud, or by the lovers' own impulsiveness — and what Shakespeare seems to think.

angleCards.title: The fever of it.
angleCards.text: This is not a slow romance. Sunday to Friday. Every decision instant, every declaration absolute. I want to feel the compression Shakespeare built into the play and understand why the speed is the point, not a flaw.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read for the speed — Romeo and Juliet are dead in five days — and what Shakespeare is saying about love that moves that fast.

angleCards.title: Mercutio as the real heart of the play.
angleCards.text: He's funnier than Romeo, clearer-eyed than anyone, and dead before the halfway point. I want to track what he represents — wit, reality, friendship — and what the play loses when he goes.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Mercutio — the wittiest, most alive character in the play — and understand what his death changes about everything that follows.

angleCards.title: Juliet is smarter than Romeo.
angleCards.text: She asks harder questions, moves more carefully, and sees what is actually at stake. I want to read the play watching her choices against his and ask whether she is undone by love or by the world she's trapped in.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Juliet as the more rational of the two lovers — the one actually thinking — and see whether Shakespeare gives her more agency than the play is usually credited for.

cast.name: Romeo
cast.description: He is in love with being in love before he ever meets Juliet. Impulsive, eloquent, and genuinely tender — but his instinct is always to act before thinking, and the play punishes him for it.

cast.name: Juliet
cast.role: The One Who Is Actually Thinking
cast.description: Thirteen years old and in most ways wiser than everyone around her. She questions, qualifies, and anticipates consequences even while falling. She is undone not by recklessness but by circumstance and other people's failures.

cast.name: Mercutio
cast.role: The Wit Who Pays For It
cast.description: Romeo's friend, the play's best speaker, and the one character who sees through romantic illusion. His death is the pivot — after it, the tone darkens and the comedy stops entirely.

cast.name: The Nurse
cast.description: Practical, bawdy, and genuinely fond of Juliet — until the moment Juliet most needs her, when she counsels compromise instead of courage. Her failure is one of the quiet tragedies inside the loud one.

cast.name: Tybalt
cast.description: He hates the Montagues purely on principle, needs no personal grievance, and cannot imagine a world where the feud ends. He is what happens when honour becomes identity.

cast.name: Friar Lawrence
cast.description: He agrees to the secret marriage because he thinks it will end the feud. His plan makes a kind of sense and fails catastrophically anyway. He is the play's argument against well-meaning adult interference.
